title: Functional Equivalence Testing
text: Classical hypothesis tests (like group.test) ask whether two groups curves different. many applications relevant question opposite: two groups curves equivalent? Examples include: Bioequivalence: generic brand-name drug produce equivalent concentration-time profiles? Process validation: new manufacturing process produce output curves within tolerance old one? Reproducibility: two labs produce equivalent functional measurements? fequiv.test() implements functional TOST (Two One-Sided Tests) procedure based supremum norm. constructs simultaneous confidence band (SCB) mean difference checks whether entire band lies within equivalence margin [−δ,δ][-\delta, \delta]. Hypotheses: H0H_0: supt|μ1(t)−μ2(t)|≥δ\sup_t |\mu_1(t) - \mu_2(t)| \geq \delta (equivalent) H1H_1: supt|μ1(t)−μ2(t)|<δ\sup_t |\mu_1(t) - \mu_2(t)| < \delta (equivalent)

title: Functional Equivalence Testing
code: library(fdars) #>  #> Attaching package: 'fdars' #> The following objects are masked from 'package:stats': #>  #>     cov, decompose, deriv, median, sd, var #> The following object is masked from 'package:base': #>  #>     norm library(ggplot2) theme_set(theme_minimal())  set.seed(42) m <- 100 t_grid <- seq(0, 1, length.out = m)

title: Functional Equivalence Testing
text: Two samples drawn distribution declared equivalent reasonable δ\delta. plot shows mean difference curve (black), simultaneous confidence band (green = equivalence declared, red = declared), equivalence margins (dashed lines ±δ\pm\delta).
code: # Two groups from the same process n1 <- 30 n2 <- 25 X1 <- matrix(0, n1, m) X2 <- matrix(0, n2, m) for (i in 1:n1) X1[i, ] <- sin(2 * pi * t_grid) + rnorm(m, sd = 0.3) for (i in 1:n2) X2[i, ] <- sin(2 * pi * t_grid) + rnorm(m, sd = 0.3)  fd1 <- fdata(X1, argvals = t_grid) fd2 <- fdata(X2, argvals = t_grid)  result <- fequiv.test(fd1, fd2, delta = 0.5, n.boot = 1000, seed = 42) print(result) #> Functional Equivalence Test (TOST) #> =================================== #> Data: fd1 and fd2  #> Two-sample test, n1 = 30 , n2 = 25  #> Bootstrap method: multiplier  #> Equivalence margin (delta): 0.5  #> Significance level (alpha): 0.05  #> --- #> Test statistic (sup|d_hat|): 0.2307  #> Critical value: 0.2708  #> SCB range: [ -0.4602 , 0.5015 ] #> P-value: 0.104  #> --- #> Decision: Fail to reject H0 -- equivalence NOT declared plot(result)

title: Functional Equivalence Testing
text: two groups genuinely different mean functions, test declare equivalence.  red band extends well beyond dashed equivalence margins, equivalence declared.
code: # Group 2 has a shifted mean X2_shifted <- matrix(0, n2, m) for (i in 1:n2) X2_shifted[i, ] <- sin(2 * pi * t_grid) + 0.8 + rnorm(m, sd = 0.3)  fd2_shifted <- fdata(X2_shifted, argvals = t_grid)  result2 <- fequiv.test(fd1, fd2_shifted, delta = 0.5, n.boot = 1000, seed = 42) print(result2) #> Functional Equivalence Test (TOST) #> =================================== #> Data: fd1 and fd2_shifted  #> Two-sample test, n1 = 30 , n2 = 25  #> Bootstrap method: multiplier  #> Equivalence margin (delta): 0.5  #> Significance level (alpha): 0.05  #> --- #> Test statistic (sup|d_hat|): 0.9969  #> Critical value: 0.2694  #> SCB range: [ -1.2663 , -0.3345 ] #> P-value: 1  #> --- #> Decision: Fail to reject H0 -- equivalence NOT declared plot(result2)

title: Functional Equivalence Testing
text: equivalence margin δ\delta maximum sup-norm difference consider scientifically negligible. must chosen looking data, based domain knowledge: large: trivially declares equivalence (low power real differences) small: almost never declares equivalence (conservative) useful diagnostic sweep δ\delta values see decision flips:
code: deltas <- seq(0.1, 1.0, by = 0.05) decisions <- sapply(deltas, function(d) {   fequiv.test(fd1, fd2, delta = d, n.boot = 500, seed = 42)$reject })  df_sweep <- data.frame(delta = deltas, equivalent = decisions) ggplot(df_sweep, aes(x = delta, y = as.numeric(equivalent))) +   geom_step(linewidth = 0.8) +   geom_point(aes(color = equivalent), size = 2) +   scale_color_manual(values = c("FALSE" = "#d62728", "TRUE" = "#2ca02c")) +   labs(x = expression(delta), y = "Equivalence declared",        title = "Decision as a function of equivalence margin") +   scale_y_continuous(breaks = c(0, 1), labels = c("No", "Yes"))

title: Functional Equivalence Testing
text: can also test whether single sample’s mean equivalent known reference function μ0\mu_0.
code: # Test if the sample mean is equivalent to the true generating function mu0 <- sin(2 * pi * t_grid) result_one <- fequiv.test(fd1, delta = 0.5, mu0 = mu0, n.boot = 1000, seed = 42) print(result_one) #> Functional Equivalence Test (TOST) #> =================================== #> Data: fd1  #> One-sample test, n = 30  #> Bootstrap method: multiplier  #> Equivalence margin (delta): 0.5  #> Significance level (alpha): 0.05  #> --- #> Test statistic (sup|d_hat|): 0.1243  #> Critical value: 0.1839  #> SCB range: [ -0.3082 , 0.2866 ] #> P-value: <2e-16  #> --- #> Decision: Reject H0 -- equivalence declared plot(result_one)

text: fequiv.test supports two bootstrap methods: "multiplier" (default): Gaussian multiplier bootstrap. Fast asymptotically valid. Recommended applications. "percentile": Resampling-based bootstrap. robust small samples heavy-tailed data.

code: tolerance_plots <- list()  for (cv in levels(cultivar)) {   idx <- which(cultivar == cv)   fd_cv <- fd_wine[idx]    # Bootstrap the trimmed mean to get a tolerance band   # Using the percentile method on pointwise quantiles of bootstrap curves   n_boot <- 500   boot_obj <- fdata.bootstrap(fd_cv, n.boot = n_boot, method = "naive",                                seed = 42)    # For each bootstrap sample, compute the trimmed mean   boot_means <- matrix(NA, n_boot, m)   for (b in seq_len(n_boot)) {     boot_means[b, ] <- as.numeric(trimmed(boot_obj$boot.samples[[b]],                                            trim = 0.25)$data)   }    # Pointwise 2.5% and 97.5% quantiles of bootstrap trimmed means   band_lower <- apply(boot_means, 2, quantile, probs = 0.025)   band_upper <- apply(boot_means, 2, quantile, probs = 0.975)    # Also compute a wider prediction band using the raw bootstrap curves   # This captures individual wine variability, not just mean uncertainty   boot_curves <- matrix(NA, n_boot, m)   for (b in seq_len(n_boot)) {     # Pick a random curve from each bootstrap sample     boot_curves[b, ] <- boot_obj$boot.samples[[b]]$data[       sample(nrow(boot_obj$boot.samples[[b]]$data), 1), ]   }   pred_lower <- apply(boot_curves, 2, quantile, probs = 0.025)   pred_upper <- apply(boot_curves, 2, quantile, probs = 0.975)    ref_mean <- as.numeric(trimmed(fd_cv, trim = 0.25)$data)    df_band <- data.frame(     t = t_grid,     mean = ref_mean,     ci_lower = band_lower, ci_upper = band_upper,     pred_lower = pred_lower, pred_upper = pred_upper   )    tolerance_plots[[cv]] <- ggplot(df_band, aes(x = t)) +     geom_ribbon(aes(ymin = pred_lower, ymax = pred_upper),                 fill = "gray80", alpha = 0.6) +     geom_ribbon(aes(ymin = ci_lower, ymax = ci_upper),                 fill = "steelblue", alpha = 0.3) +     geom_line(aes(y = mean), color = "navy", linewidth = 1) +     labs(title = sprintf("%s (n = %d)", cv, length(idx)),          subtitle = "Navy = trimmed mean, Blue = 95% CI of mean, Gray = 95% prediction band",          x = expression(t), y = expression(f[x](t))) +     theme_minimal() }  tolerance_plots[["Barolo"]] / tolerance_plots[["Grignolino"]] / tolerance_plots[["Barbera"]]

what: Comparison: What Would Standard Statistics Give You?
title: Andrews Wine: Outlier Detection
text: classically trained analyst might reach Mahalanobis distance — standard multivariate outlier detector. measures far wine population mean, accounting correlations chemicals. Wines exceeding χ2\chi^2 critical value flagged. Mahalanobis vs FDA: flagged wines compared overlap substantial — distance preservation theorem predicts, approaches working underlying Euclidean geometry. notice difference get: Mahalanobis distance fine screening tool, dataset largely agrees FDA methods. flags Wine 122 distance 58.7, can’t tell — every chemical extreme, pattern unusual? FDA approach answers : depth-ponderation says wine far population center, outliergram says shape unusual, magnitude-shape plot says chemical ratios aren’t distorted. quality controller, distinction means difference re-running test (magnitude issue) investigating vineyard (shape issue).
code:
# Classical Mahalanobis distance outlier detection mahal <- mahalanobis(X, colMeans(X), cov(X)) cutoff_chi <- qchisq(0.975, df = ncol(X)) mahal_outliers <- which(mahal > cutoff_chi)  cat(sprintf("Mahalanobis outliers (chi-sq cutoff = %.1f, df = %d):
",             cutoff_chi, ncol(X))) #> Mahalanobis outliers (chi-sq cutoff = 24.7, df = 13): cat("  Flagged:", sort(mahal_outliers), "
") #>   Flagged: 14 60 70 72 74 96 97 111 116 122 159 160 cat("  Count:", length(mahal_outliers), "
") #>   Count: 12 # Compare with FDA results fda_all <- unique(c(out_pond$outliers, og$outliers, ms$outliers)) overlap <- intersect(mahal_outliers, fda_all) fda_only <- setdiff(fda_all, mahal_outliers) mahal_only <- setdiff(mahal_outliers, fda_all)  cat("Overlap between methods:
") #> Overlap between methods: cat("  Both flag:           ", sort(overlap), "
") #>   Both flag:            60 70 74 96 97 111 122 159 cat("  FDA only:            ", sort(fda_only), "
") #>   FDA only:             79 cat("  Mahalanobis only:    ", sort(mahal_only), "
") #>   Mahalanobis only:     14 72 116 160  # Show Mahalanobis distances for FDA-flagged wines compare_df <- data.frame(   Wine = sort(union(mahal_outliers, fda_all)),   Cultivar = as.character(cultivar[sort(union(mahal_outliers, fda_all))]) ) compare_df$Mahal_Dist <- round(mahal[compare_df$Wine], 1) compare_df$Mahal_Flag <- compare_df$Wine %in% mahal_outliers compare_df$FDA_Flag <- compare_df$Wine %in% fda_all compare_df$FDA_Methods <- sapply(compare_df$Wine, function(w) {   methods <- c()   if (w %in% out_pond$outliers) methods <- c(methods, "Depth")   if (w %in% og$outliers) methods <- c(methods, "Outliergram")   if (w %in% ms$outliers) methods <- c(methods, "MS-plot")   paste(methods, collapse = " + ") })  kable(compare_df, caption = "Mahalanobis vs FDA: flagged wines compared")

data(growth_vel, package = "fdasrvf")  # growth_vel$f is 69 (grid) x 93 (curves) — transpose for fdata # Standard ordering: first 39 = boys, last 54 = girls fd_growth_raw <- fdata(t(growth_vel$f), argvals = growth_vel$time) gender <- factor(c(rep("Boy", 39), rep("Girl", 54))) cat("Curves:", nrow(fd_growth_raw$data),     "(", sum(gender == "Boy"), "boys,", sum(gender == "Girl"), "girls)
") #> Curves: 93 ( 39 boys, 54 girls) cat("Grid points:", ncol(fd_growth_raw$data), "
") #> Grid points: 69 cat("Age range:", range(fd_growth_raw$argvals), "

what: Testing the Gender Difference in Timing
title: Berkeley Growth Study: Elastic Alignment of Growth Velocity
text: visual pattern suggests boys girls differ pubertal timing. can test formally fequiv.test(), checks whether mean warping functions two groups equivalent within margin δ\delta. equivalence declared, evidence timing patterns genuinely differ. use δ=0.5\delta = 0.5 years – differences smaller half year considered practically negligible:  mean difference curve (solid line) simultaneous confidence band (shaded) far exceed ±δ=0.5\pm\delta = 0.5 year margins (dashed lines), equivalence decisively rejected. mean warping functions group show separation directly:  Girls’ mean warping sits identity (growth spurt features occur younger ages), boys’ sits . vertical gap two curves represents timing difference reference age. can quantify timing gap directly original curves: equivalence test warping functions confirms peak ages show: boys girls meaningfully different growth timing.

warps_boys <- km_pub$gammas[gender == "Boy"] warps_girls <- km_pub$gammas[gender == "Girl"]  set.seed(42) equiv <- fequiv.test(warps_boys, warps_girls, delta = 0.5,                      n.boot = 1000, title: Functional Principal Component Analysis (FPCA)
text: working functional data, face several challenges: High dimensionality: curve observed many points Infinite-dimensional nature: Curves live function spaces Correlation structure: Points curve highly correlated Noise: Observations contain measurement error FPCA addresses challenges finding principal modes variation data—orthogonal functions capture curves differ .

title: Functional Principal Component Analysis (FPCA)
text: square-integrable random function X(t)X(t) can represented : X(t)=μ(t)+∑k=1∞ξkϕk(t)X(t) = \mu(t) + \sum_{k=1}^{\infty} \xi_k \phi_k(t) : μ(t)\mu(t) mean function ϕk(t)\phi_k(t) eigenfunctions (functional principal components) ξk\xi_k scores (random coefficients) eigenfunctions satisfy: ∫C(s,t)ϕk(s)ds=λkϕk(t)\int C(s, t) \phi_k(s) \, ds = \lambda_k \phi_k(t) C(s,t)=Cov(X(s),X(t))C(s, t) = \text{Cov}(X(s), X(t)) covariance function λk\lambda_k eigenvalues (variances explained component).

title: Functional Principal Component Analysis (FPCA)
text: Orthonormality: ∫ϕj(t)ϕk(t)dt=δjk\int \phi_j(t) \phi_k(t) \, dt = \delta_{jk} Uncorrelated scores: Cov(ξj,ξk)=λjδjk\text{Cov}(\xi_j, \xi_k) = \lambda_j \delta_{jk} Optimal reconstruction: FPCA minimizes integrated squared error fixed number components Variance ordering: λ1≥λ2≥⋯≥0\lambda_1 \geq \lambda_2 \geq \cdots \geq 0

title: Functional Principal Component Analysis (FPCA)
text: Let’s demonstrate FPCA simulated growth data showing different growth patterns.
code: # Simulate growth curves with two main modes of variation n <- 50 m <- 100 t <- seq(0, 18, length.out = m)  # Age 0-18 years  # Base growth pattern (logistic-like) base_growth <- function(t) 50 + 130 / (1 + exp(-0.5 * (t - 10)))  # Generate curves with: # - Overall height variation (PC1: taller/shorter) # - Growth timing variation (PC2: earlier/later maturation) X <- matrix(0, n, m) height_effect <- rnorm(n, sd = 10)      # Individual height differences timing_effect <- rnorm(n, sd = 1.5)     # Individual timing differences  for (i in 1:n) {   shifted_t <- t - timing_effect[i]   X[i, ] <- base_growth(shifted_t) + height_effect[i] + rnorm(m, sd = 2) }  fd <- fdata(X, argvals = t) plot(fd) +   labs(x = "Age (years)", y = "Height (cm)", title = "Simulated Growth Curves")

title: Functional Principal Component Analysis (FPCA)
text: fdata2pc() function computes functional principal components: output shows: Singular values: Related importance component Variance explained: Percentage total variance captured PC Cumulative variance: Running total—often aim 90-95%
code: # Extract first 4 principal components fpca <- fdata2pc(fd, ncomp = 4) print(fpca) #> Functional Principal Component Analysis #> ======================================== #> Number of observations: 50  #> Number of components: 4  #>  #> Variance explained: #>   PC1: 92.4% (cumulative: 92.4%) #>   PC2: 5.9% (cumulative: 98.3%) #>   PC3: 1.6% (cumulative: 99.9%) #>   PC4: 0.1% (cumulative: 100.0%)

title: Functional Principal Component Analysis (FPCA)
text: plot() method type = "components" shows PC affects mean curve. component displayed facet clear comparison:  facet shows one principal component solid lines differentiated color: Black: Mean function μ(t)\mu(t) Blue: Mean + perturbation (μ+c⋅ϕk\mu + c \cdot \phi_k) Coral: Mean - perturbation (μ−c⋅ϕk\mu - c \cdot \phi_k) c=2×λkc = 2 \times \sqrt{\lambda_k} scales perturbation component’s importance. can show positive perturbation setting show_both_directions = FALSE:  Interpretation: PC1: Overall height differences (taller vs shorter individuals) PC2: Growth timing (earlier vs later maturation) PC3: subtle shape variations

title: Supervised Classification of Functional Data
text: fundamental problem : given curve Xi(t)X_i(t), predict class label gi∈{1,…,G}g_i \\{1, \ldots, G\}. One might tempted discretize curve mm grid points apply standard multivariate classifier. However, approach faces two obstacles: Curse dimensionality. mm grid points (often 100–1000), multivariate classifiers struggle unless n≫mn \gg m. Covariance matrices become singular, nearest-neighbor distances concentrate, decision boundaries overfit. Ignoring smoothness. Discretization treats Xi(t1)X_i(t_1) Xi(t2)X_i(t_2) unrelated features, discarding continuity smoothness underlying curves. Functional classification resolves first projecting curves onto low-dimensional basis — typically leading FPC directions — classifying reduced space. simultaneously regularizes problem (since K≪mK \ll m) respects functional structure (since FPCs capture dominant modes variation). methods work directly function space (kernel classifier, DD classifier), distances computed using proper functional metrics (L2L^2 norm depth), avoiding discretization artifacts entirely.

title: Supervised Classification of Functional Data
text: FPC-based methods (LDA, QDA, kNN) start computing scores 𝛏i=(ξi1,…,ξiK)T\boldsymbol\xi_i = (\xi_{i1}, \ldots, \xi_{iK})^T ξik=∫[Xi(t)−X‾(t)]ϕk(t)dt\xi_{ik} = \int [X_i(t) - \bar{X}(t)]\phi_k(t)\,dt ϕk\phi_k eigenfunctions pooled covariance operator. Classification operates ℝK\mathbb{R}^K.

title: Supervised Classification of Functional Data
text: LDA assumes FPC scores within class Gaussian common covariance: 𝛏∣g=k∼𝒩(𝛍k,𝚺pool)\boldsymbol\xi \mid g = k \;\sim\; \mathcal{N}(\boldsymbol\mu_k,\, \boldsymbol\Sigma_{\text{pool}}) pooled covariance : 𝚺̂pool=1n−G∑g=1G∑∈g(𝛏i−𝛏‾g)(𝛏i−𝛏‾g)T\hat{\boldsymbol\Sigma}_{\text{pool}} = \frac{1}{n - G}\sum_{g=1}^G \sum_{\g}(\boldsymbol\xi_i - \bar{\boldsymbol\xi}_g)(\boldsymbol\xi_i - \bar{\boldsymbol\xi}_g)^T Classification uses log-posterior discriminant: δg(𝛏)=logπg−12(𝛏−𝛍g)T𝚺pool−1(𝛏−𝛍g)\delta_g(\boldsymbol\xi) = \log\pi_g - \tfrac{1}{2}(\boldsymbol\xi - \boldsymbol\mu_g)^T \boldsymbol\Sigma_{\text{pool}}^{-1}(\boldsymbol\xi - \boldsymbol\mu_g) πg\pi_g prior probability class gg (estimated class proportions). observation assigned ĝ=argmaxgδg(𝛏)\hat{g} = \arg\max_g \delta_g(\boldsymbol\xi). 𝚺pool\boldsymbol\Sigma_{\text{pool}} shared, decision boundaries linear (hyperplanes) FPC score space.

title: Supervised Classification of Functional Data
text: QDA relaxes equal-covariance assumption estimating class-specific covariance 𝚺g\boldsymbol\Sigma_g group. discriminant becomes: δg(𝛏)=logπg−12log|𝚺g|−12(𝛏−𝛍g)T𝚺g−1(𝛏−𝛍g)\delta_g(\boldsymbol\xi) = \log\pi_g - \tfrac{1}{2}\log|\boldsymbol\Sigma_g| - \tfrac{1}{2}(\boldsymbol\xi - \boldsymbol\mu_g)^T\boldsymbol\Sigma_g^{-1}(\boldsymbol\xi - \boldsymbol\mu_g) additional log|𝚺g|\log|\boldsymbol\Sigma_g| term penalizes classes large spread. Decision boundaries now quadratic (ellipsoidal). QDA flexible LDA requires enough observations per class reliably estimate 𝚺g\boldsymbol\Sigma_g — roughly ng>K(K+1)/2n_g > K(K+1)/2 rule thumb.

title: Supervised Classification of Functional Data
text: kNN classifies majority vote among kk closest training curves FPC space, using Euclidean distance: d(𝛏i,𝛏j)=∥𝛏i−𝛏j∥2=∑l=1K(ξil−ξjl)2d(\boldsymbol\xi_i, \boldsymbol\xi_j) = \|\boldsymbol\xi_i - \boldsymbol\xi_j\|_2 = \sqrt{\sum_{l=1}^K (\xi_{il} - \xi_{jl})^2} predicted class whichever label appears often among kk neighbors. kNN makes distributional assumptions, making robust non-Gaussian score distributions nonlinear class boundaries. choice kk typically made via cross-validation: small kk gives flexible noisy boundaries; large kk gives smoother potentially biased boundaries.

title: Supervised Classification of Functional Data
text: kernel classifier works directly function space without dimension reduction. uses L2L^2 functional distance Simpson’s rule integration weights: d(Xi,Xj)=∫01[Xi(t)−Xj(t)]2dtd(X_i, X_j) = \sqrt{\int_0^1 [X_i(t) - X_j(t)]^2\,dt} Classification uses Gaussian kernel weight contributions training curves: K(d,h)=exp(−d22h2)K(d, h) = \exp\!\left(-\frac{d^2}{2h^2}\right) predicted class : ĝ(X)=argmaxg∑j:yj=gK(d(X,Xj),h)\hat{g}(X) = \arg\max_g \sum_{j:\,y_j = g} K\bigl(d(X, X_j),\, h\bigr) , class, kernel weights training curves class summed, class largest total weight wins. bandwidth hh controls locality classifier. fclassif() selects hh via leave-one-cross-validation grid distance percentiles.

title: Supervised Classification of Functional Data
text: depth-based classifier avoids dimension reduction distance computation. Instead, computes statistical depth curve respect class distribution: Dg(Xi)=depth Xi w.r.t. class gD_g(X_i) = \text{depth } X_i \text{ w.r.t. class } g using Fraiman–Muniz integrated depth: DFM(X)=∫01D1(X(t);Ft)dtD_{\text{FM}}(X) = \int_0^1 D_1\bigl(X(t);\, F_t\bigr)\,dt D1D_1 univariate depth (one minus twice distance median CDF value) FtF_t marginal distribution time tt. GG classes, curve mapped point (D1(Xi),…,DG(Xi))∈ℝG(D_1(X_i), \ldots, D_G(X_i)) \\mathbb{R}^G classification proceeds “depth-depth” space. simplest rule assigns ĝ=argmaxgDg(Xi)\hat{g} = \arg\max_g D_g(X_i): class curve “central”. approach robust outliers depth rank-based measure.

title: Supervised Classification of Functional Data
text: Instead toy simulation use classic iris dataset, transformed functional data via Andrews transformation. maps 4-dimensional observation curve [−π,π][-\pi, \pi] using Fourier expansion — preserving Euclidean distances constant factor. three species (setosa, versicolor, virginica) classes. Crucially, versicolor virginica overlap substantially, making non-trivial classification task.  Setosa well separated, versicolor virginica overlap — exactly kind challenge classifier choice matters.
code: andrews_transform <- function(X, m = 200) {   if (is.data.frame(X)) X <- as.matrix(X)   n <- nrow(X)   p <- ncol(X)   t_grid <- seq(-pi, pi, length.out = m)    basis <- matrix(0, m, p)   basis[, 1] <- 1 / sqrt(2)   for (j in 2:p) {     k <- ceiling((j - 1) / 2)     if (j %% 2 == 0) {       basis[, j] <- sin(k * t_grid)     } else {       basis[, j] <- cos(k * t_grid)     }   }    fdata(X %*% t(basis), argvals = t_grid) } X_raw <- as.matrix(iris[, 1:4]) X <- scale(X_raw) species <- iris$Species y <- as.integer(species)  # 1 = setosa, 2 = versicolor, 3 = virginica  fd <- andrews_transform(X) plot(fd, color = species, alpha = 0.35, show.mean = TRUE,      palette = c("setosa" = "#E69F00", "versicolor" = "#56B4E9",                  "virginica" = "#009E73")) +   labs(x = expression(t), y = expression(f[x](t)),        title = "Iris Andrews Curves by Species")

what: Why Mixed Models for Functional Data?
title: Functional Mixed Models for Repeated Measures
text: subjects contribute multiple curves, observations longer independent. Ignoring structure serious consequences: Pseudoreplication. Treating ntotaln_{\text{total}} curves independent inflates effective sample size. Standard errors small, p-values optimistic, Type error rates exceed nominal level. Confounding sources variation. Without subject-level random effects, -subject variability absorbed residual, blurring distinction “subjects differ” “measurements noisy.” Inefficient estimation. within-subject correlation carries information fixed effects. Mixed models exploit correlation structure, producing efficient (lower-variance) estimates methods ignore . functional mixed model resolves issues decomposing curve four additive components: decomposition functional analog classical scalar linear mixed model yij=μ+xijTβ+bi+εijy_{ij} = \mu + x_{ij}^T\beta + b_i + \varepsilon_{ij}, scalar parameter replaced function tt.

title: Functional Mixed Models for Repeated Measures
text: full model jj-th observation subject ii : Yij(t)=μ(t)+∑p=1Pβp(t)xip+bi(t)+εij(t)Y_{ij}(t) = \mu(t) + \sum_{p=1}^P \beta_p(t)\,x_{ip} + b_i(t) + \varepsilon_{ij}(t) distributional assumptions: bi(t)∼GP(0,σu2)b_i(t) \sim \text{GP}(0, \sigma^2_u): subject-specific random effects, independent across subjects εij(t)∼GP(0,σε2)\varepsilon_{ij}(t) \sim \text{GP}(0, \sigma^2_\varepsilon): residual noise, independent across observations GP denotes Gaussian process. key parameters two variance components σu2\sigma^2_u (-subject) σε2\sigma^2_\varepsilon (within-subject).

title: Functional Mixed Models for Repeated Measures
text: Direct estimation functional parameters μ(t),βp(t),bi(t)\mu(t), \beta_p(t), b_i(t) infinite-dimensional. FPC approach reduces set scalar mixed models. Step 1. Compute FPC decomposition pooled data: Yij(t)−Y‾(t)≈∑k=1Kξij,kϕk(t)Y_{ij}(t) - \bar{Y}(t) \approx \sum_{k=1}^K \xi_{ij,k}\,\phi_k(t) ϕk(t)\phi_k(t) eigenfunctions ξij,k\xi_{ij,k} scores. Step 2. component k=1,…,Kk = 1, \ldots, K, fit scalar mixed model: ξij,k=γ0k+∑p=1Pγpkxip+uik+eijk\xi_{ij,k} = \gamma_{0k} + \sum_{p=1}^P \gamma_{pk}\,x_{ip} + u_{ik} + e_{ijk} uik∼𝒩(0,σu,k2)u_{ik} \sim \mathcal{N}(0, \sigma^2_{u,k}) subject-level random effects eijk∼𝒩(0,σε,k2)e_{ijk} \sim \mathcal{N}(0, \sigma^2_{\varepsilon,k}) residuals. Step 3. Reconstruct functional parameters: μ̂(t)=Y‾(t)+∑kγ̂0kϕk(t),β̂p(t)=∑kγ̂pkϕk(t)\hat\mu(t) = \bar{Y}(t) + \sum_k \hat\gamma_{0k}\,\phi_k(t), \qquad \hat\beta_p(t) = \sum_k \hat\gamma_{pk}\,\phi_k(t) b̂(t)=∑kûikϕk(t)\hat{b}_i(t) = \sum_k \hat{u}_{ik}\,\phi_k(t) approach elegant: infinite-dimensional functional mixed model decomposes KK independent scalar mixed models, can fitted using standard REML estimation.

title: Functional Mixed Models for Repeated Measures
text: Within FPC component, variance components estimated via Restricted Maximum Likelihood (REML), accounts loss degrees freedom estimating fixed effects. key quantities : Shrinkage weights: wi=σu2σu2+σε2/niw_i = \frac{\sigma^2_u}{\sigma^2_u + \sigma^2_\varepsilon / n_i} nin_i number observations subject ii. nin_i large σu2≫σε2\sigma^2_u \gg \sigma^2_\varepsilon, wi≈1w_i \approx 1 random effect estimate close raw subject mean. nin_i small σu2≪σε2\sigma^2_u \ll \sigma^2_\varepsilon, wi≈0w_i \approx 0 estimate shrunk toward zero (population mean). BLUP (Best Linear Unbiased Predictor) random effects: û=wi(ξ‾−x‾iTγ̂)\hat{u}_i = w_i\bigl(\bar{\xi}_i - \bar{x}_i^T\hat\gamma\bigr) BLUP “borrows strength” across subjects: subjects observations pulled toward population mean, subjects many observations retain individual character. functional analog well-known shrinkage property scalar mixed models. REML divisor: variance estimate uses n−pn - p denominator (pp number fixed-effect parameters) rather nn, correcting bias otherwise arise estimating fixed effects variance components simultaneously.

title: Functional Mixed Models for Repeated Measures
text: Testing whether covariate significant functional effect: H0:βp(t)=0 tH_0: \beta_p(t) = 0 \text{ } t analogous functional ANOVA. test uses permutation approach respects within-subject correlation: Compute observed F-statistic FobsF_{\text{obs}} fitted model. b=1,…,Bb = 1, \ldots, B: permute subject-level labels (individual observations) refit model obtain Fb*F_b^*. p-value : p=1+#{Fb*≥Fobs}B+1p = \frac{1 + \#\{F_b^* \geq F_{\text{obs}}\}}{B + 1} Permuting subject level (rather observation level) preserves within-subject correlation structure null hypothesis, ensuring valid inference even complex dependency patterns.

title: Functional Mixed Models for Repeated Measures
text: simulate clinical trial 15 subjects, measured 3 time points, binary treatment covariate. simulation three variance sources: treatment effect (0.5cos(2πt)0.5\cos(2\pi t) treated subjects), subject-level random effects (smooth random curves σ≈0.3\sigma \approx 0.3), measurement noise (σ=0.1\sigma = 0.1). model recover components.
code: set.seed(42) n_subjects <- 15 n_visits <- 3 n_total <- n_subjects * n_visits m <- 80 t_grid <- seq(0, 1, length.out = m)  # Subject-specific random effects subject_effects <- matrix(0, n_subjects, m) for (i in 1:n_subjects) {   subject_effects[i, ] <- 0.3 * rnorm(1) * sin(2 * pi * t_grid) +     0.2 * rnorm(1) * cos(4 * pi * t_grid) }  # Treatment assignment (first 8 subjects treated, rest control) treatment <- c(rep(1, 8), rep(0, 7))  # Generate observations Y <- matrix(0, n_total, m) subject_ids <- rep(1:n_subjects, each = n_visits) covariates <- matrix(0, n_total, 1)  for (i in 1:n_total) {   subj <- subject_ids[i]   trt <- treatment[subj]   covariates[i, 1] <- trt    Y[i, ] <- sin(2 * pi * t_grid) +                         # Mean function     trt * 0.5 * cos(2 * pi * t_grid) +                      # Treatment effect     subject_effects[subj, ] +                                 # Random effect     rnorm(m, sd = 0.1)                                        # Noise }  fd <- fdata(Y, argvals = t_grid)

title: Functional Regression: Scalar and Function Responses
text: Functional regression extends classical regression settings predictors responses functions. fdars provides two complementary directions: Scalar--function regression: scalar response, functional predictors (fregre.lm(), functional.logistic()) Function--scalar regression: functional response, scalar predictors (fosr(), fosr.fpc(), fanova()) article demonstrates , including cross-validation hypothesis testing.
code: library(fdars) #>  #> Attaching package: 'fdars' #> The following objects are masked from 'package:stats': #>  #>     cov, decompose, deriv, median, sd, var #> The following object is masked from 'package:base': #>  #>     norm library(ggplot2) theme_set(theme_minimal())

title: Functional Regression: Scalar and Function Responses
text: Classical regression assumes predictors live ℝp\mathbb{R}^p pp finite fixed. predictor curve Xi(t)X_i(t) observed continuum, face fundamentally different problem: regression coefficient β(t)\beta(t) function, “design matrix” infinite-dimensional. creates two immediate challenges: Ill-posedness. functional linear model yi=α+∫Xi(t)β(t)dt+εiy_i = \alpha + \int X_i(t)\beta(t)\,dt + \varepsilon_i infinitely many solutions integral operator compact. Without regularization, least-squares estimate β(t)\beta(t) exist wildly unstable. Curse dimensionality. Naively discretizing Xi(t)X_i(t) mm grid points running OLS gives mm parameters nn observations. m≫nm \gg n (typical FDA setting), model massively overparameterized. Two strategies resolve issues: Dimension reduction: project Xi(t)X_i(t) onto leading functional principal components (FPCs) regress scores. approach taken fregre.lm() fregre.pc(). Penalization: estimate β(t)\beta(t) directly penalize roughness via second-derivative penalty. approach taken fosr() function--scalar direction. approaches replace ill-posed infinite-dimensional problem well-conditioned finite-dimensional one.

title: Functional Regression: Scalar and Function Responses
text: functional linear model relates scalar response yiy_i functional predictor Xi(t)X_i(t) via: yi=α+∫01Xi(t)β(t)dt+εi,εi∼iid(0,σ2)y_i = \alpha + \int_0^1 X_i(t)\,\beta(t)\,dt + \varepsilon_i, \quad \varepsilon_i \overset{\text{iid}}{\sim} (0, \sigma^2) coefficient function β(t)\beta(t) describes predictor curve time tt influences response. positive β(t)\beta(t) interval means curves higher values tend higher yiy_i.

title: Functional Regression: Scalar and Function Responses
text: Let ϕ1(t),ϕ2(t),…\phi_1(t), \phi_2(t), \ldots eigenfunctions covariance operator XX, let ξik=∫(Xi(t)−X‾(t))ϕk(t)dt\xi_{ik} = \int (X_i(t) - \bar{X}(t))\phi_k(t)\,dt FPC scores. Expanding β(t)=∑k=1∞γkϕk(t)\beta(t) = \sum_{k=1}^\infty \gamma_k \phi_k(t) substituting gives: yi≈α+∑k=1Kγkξik+εiy_i \approx \alpha + \sum_{k=1}^K \gamma_k \xi_{ik} + \varepsilon_i reduces functional regression ordinary multiple regression KK FPC scores. coefficient function recovered : β̂(t)=∑k=1Kγ̂kϕk(t)\hat\beta(t) = \sum_{k=1}^K \hat\gamma_k \phi_k(t) number components KK controls bias–variance trade-: components oversimplify β(t)\beta(t); many introduce noise. Cross-validation selects KK data-driven way.

title: Functional Regression: Scalar and Function Responses
text: FPC scores predictors, standard OLS inference applies. variance γ̂\hat\gamma σ2(ΞTΞ)−1\sigma^2 (\Xi^T\Xi)^{-1} Ξ\Xi n×Kn \times K score matrix. Generalized cross-validation provides computationally efficient alternative leave-one-CV: GCV=1n∑=1n(yi−ŷi1−hii)2\text{GCV} = \frac{1}{n}\sum_{=1}^n \left(\frac{y_i - \hat{y}_i}{1 - h_{ii}}\right)^2 hiih_{ii} diagonal elements hat matrix H=Ξ(ΞTΞ)−1ΞTH = \Xi(\Xi^T\Xi)^{-1}\Xi^T.

title: Functional Regression: Scalar and Function Responses
text: fregre.lm() estimates β(t)\beta(t) projecting onto functional principal components. R-squared tells us much scalar variance explained leading FPC directions predictor curves. estimated β̂(t)\hat\beta(t) approximate true β(t)=sin(2πt)\beta(t) = \sin(2\pi t) used simulation.
code: set.seed(42) n <- 80 m <- 100 t_grid <- seq(0, 1, length.out = m)  # Simulate functional predictor X <- matrix(0, n, m) for (i in 1:n) {   X[i, ] <- sin(2 * pi * t_grid) * runif(1, 0.5, 2) +     cos(4 * pi * t_grid) * rnorm(1, sd = 0.3) +     rnorm(m, sd = 0.1) }  # Scalar response depends on the first FPC direction beta_true <- sin(2 * pi * t_grid) y <- X %*% beta_true / m + rnorm(n, sd = 0.3)  fd <- fdata(X, argvals = t_grid) fit <- fregre.lm(fd, y, ncomp = 3) print(fit) #> Functional Linear Model (FPC-based) #> ==================================== #>   Number of observations: 80  #>   Number of FPC components: 3  #>   R-squared: 0.4371  #>   Adjusted R-squared: 0.4149  #>   GCV: 0.0968

title: Functional Regression: Scalar and Function Responses
text: fregre.lm.cv() selects optimal number FPC components via k-fold cross-validation. data-driven way choose KK, balancing approximation accuracy overfitting. CV error typically decreases components added (capturing signal), plateaus increases (adding noise). optimal KK sits elbow.
code: cv_result <- fregre.lm.cv(fd, y, k.range = 1:8, nfold = 10) cat("Optimal ncomp:", cv_result$optimal.k, "\n") #> Optimal ncomp: 6 cat("CV errors:", round(cv_result$cv.errors, 4), "\n") #> CV errors: 0.0957 0.0959 0.0971 0.0971 0.0978 0.0938 0.0942 0.0951

title: Functional Regression: Scalar and Function Responses
text: functional logistic model uses logit link FPC scores: logP(Yi=1)1−P(Yi=1)=α+∑k=1Kγkξik\log\frac{P(Y_i = 1)}{1 - P(Y_i = 1)} = \alpha + \sum_{k=1}^K \gamma_k \xi_{ik} estimated via Iteratively Reweighted Least Squares (IRLS), alternates : Working response: zi=η̂+(yi−p̂)/[p̂(1−p̂)]z_i = \hat\eta_i + (y_i - \hat{p}_i) / [\hat{p}_i(1 - \hat{p}_i)] Working weights: wi=p̂(1−p̂)w_i = \hat{p}_i(1 - \hat{p}_i) Weighted least squares: update γ̂\hat\gamma regressing zz Ξ\Xi weights ww Convergence monitored via log-likelihood: ℓ(γ)=∑=1n[yilogpi+(1−yi)log(1−pi)]\ell(\gamma) = \sum_{=1}^n \bigl[y_i \log p_i + (1 - y_i)\log(1 - p_i)\bigr] pi=logit−1(α+ξiTγ)p_i = \text{logit}^{-1}(\alpha + \xi_i^T\gamma). estimated probabilities near 0 1 indicate confident classification; values near 0.5 indicate curves overlap region predictor’s FPC scores clearly separate two classes.
code: # Create binary response (0/1) y_bin <- as.numeric(y > median(y))  logit_fit <- functional.logistic(fd, y_bin, ncomp = 3) print(logit_fit) #> Functional Logistic Regression #> ============================== #>   Number of observations: 80  #>   Number of FPC components: 3  #>   Accuracy: 0.85  #>   Log-likelihood: -30.93  #>   Iterations: 6  cat("Probabilities range:", range(logit_fit$probabilities), "\n") #> Probabilities range: 0.01257656 0.9824597

title: Functional Regression: Scalar and Function Responses
text: response function predictors scalar, model : Yi(t)=μ(t)+∑j=1pxijβj(t)+εi(t)Y_i(t) = \mu(t) + \sum_{j=1}^p x_{ij}\,\beta_j(t) + \varepsilon_i(t) coefficient βj(t)\beta_j(t) function describing predictor jj modifies response curve time point tt. intercept μ(t)\mu(t) mean response predictors zero.

title: Functional Regression: Scalar and Function Responses
text: Direct pointwise OLS tt produce coefficient estimates noisy discontinuous across time domain. fosr() imposes smoothness via second-difference roughness penalty. penalized objective : ∑=1n∥Yi−μ−Xiβ∥2+λ∑j=1p∫[βj″(t)]2dt\sum_{=1}^n \|Y_i - \mu - X_i\beta\|^2 + \lambda \sum_{j=1}^p \int [\beta_j''(t)]^2\,dt λ>0\lambda > 0 controls trade-fidelity data smoothness. matrix form, penalty uses second-difference matrix DD: β̂=argminβ∥Y−Xβ∥F2+λtr(βTDTDβ)\hat\beta = \arg\min_\beta \|Y - X\beta\|_F^2 + \lambda\,\text{tr}(\beta^T D^T D\,\beta) solution grid point ridge-type estimator: β̂(⋅)=(XTX+λDTD)−1XTY(⋅)\hat\beta(\cdot) = (X^TX + \lambda D^TD)^{-1} X^T Y(\cdot)

title: Functional Regression: Scalar and Function Responses
text: goodness fit measured pointwise R-squared: R2(t)=1−∑[Yi(t)−Ŷ(t)]2∑[Yi(t)−Y‾(t)]2R^2(t) = 1 - \frac{\sum_i [Y_i(t) - \hat{Y}_i(t)]^2}{\sum_i [Y_i(t) - \bar{Y}(t)]^2} overall (mean) R-squared averages across domain. Values near 1 everywhere indicate scalar predictors explain functional response well time points; regions low R2(t)R^2(t) suggest additional predictors nonlinear effects may needed.

title: Functional Regression: Scalar and Function Responses
text: fosr() estimates coefficient functions βj(t)\beta_j(t) optional ridge penalty. treatment coefficient β̂1(t)\hat\beta_1(t) recover simulated 0.5cos(2πt)0.5\cos(2\pi t) pattern, age coefficient β̂2(t)\hat\beta_2(t) approximate linear 0.2t0.2t trend.
code: set.seed(42) n <- 60 m <- 80 t_grid <- seq(0, 1, length.out = m)  # Two scalar predictors: treatment and age treatment <- rep(c(0, 1), each = n/2) age <- rnorm(n) predictors <- cbind(treatment, age)  # Functional response depends on predictors Y <- matrix(0, n, m) for (i in 1:n) {   Y[i, ] <- sin(2 * pi * t_grid) +     treatment[i] * 0.5 * cos(2 * pi * t_grid) +     age[i] * 0.2 * t_grid +     rnorm(m, sd = 0.15) }  fd_y <- fdata(Y, argvals = t_grid) fosr_fit <- fosr(fd_y, predictors, lambda = 0.1) print(fosr_fit) #> Function-on-Scalar Regression #> ============================= #>   Number of observations: 60  #>   Number of predictors: 2  #>   Evaluation points: 80  #>   R-squared: 0.6412  #>   Lambda: 0.1

text: Functional ANOVA tests whether mean functions GG groups equal: H0:μ1(t)=μ2(t)=⋯=μG(t)tH_0: \mu_1(t) = \mu_2(t) = \cdots = \mu_G(t) \quad \text{} t grid point tt, pointwise F-statistic computed: F(t)=∑g=1Gng[Y‾g(t)−Y‾(t)]2/(G−1)∑g=1G∑∈g[Yi(t)−Y‾g(t)]2/(N−G)F(t) = \frac{\sum_{g=1}^G n_g [\bar{Y}_g(t) - \bar{Y}(t)]^2 / (G - 1)}{\sum_{g=1}^G \sum_{\g} [Y_i(t) - \bar{Y}_g(t)]^2 / (N - G)} summarized global test statistic integration: Fglobal=∫F(t)dtF_{\text{global}} = \int F(t)\,dt

text: null distribution FglobalF_{\text{global}} intractable, fanova() uses permutation approach: Compute observed FobsF_{\text{obs}} original data. b=1,…,Bb = 1, \ldots, B: randomly permute group labels compute Fb*F_b^*. p-value : p=1+#{Fb*≥Fobs}B+1p = \frac{1 + \#\{F_b^* \geq F_{\text{obs}}\}}{B + 1} +1+1 numerator denominator ensures p-value never exactly zero accounts observed statistic one B+1B + 1 values consideration. makes test exact (valid sample size) assumption-free regarding distribution εi(t)\varepsilon_i(t).

title: Functional Regression: Scalar and Function Responses
text: fanova() tests whether mean functions differ across groups using permutation-based F-test. small p-value rejects null hypothesis groups share mean function. simulation, three groups clearly different shapes (sine, sine + cosine, linear), expect strong rejection.
code: set.seed(42) n_per_group <- 25 m <- 80 t_grid <- seq(0, 1, length.out = m)  # Three treatment groups with different mean functions Y_anova <- matrix(0, 3 * n_per_group, m) for (i in 1:n_per_group) {   Y_anova[i, ] <- sin(2 * pi * t_grid) + rnorm(m, sd = 0.15)   Y_anova[n_per_group + i, ] <- sin(2 * pi * t_grid) + 0.5 * cos(2 * pi * t_grid) +     rnorm(m, sd = 0.15)   Y_anova[2 * n_per_group + i, ] <- 2 * t_grid - 1 + rnorm(m, sd = 0.15) } groups <- rep(1:3, each = n_per_group)  fd_anova <- fdata(Y_anova, argvals = t_grid) anova_result <- fanova(fd_anova, groups, n.perm = 500) print(anova_result) #> Functional ANOVA #> ================ #>   Number of groups: 3  #>   Number of observations: 75  #>   Global F-statistic: 577.3765  #>   P-value: 0.001996  #>   Permutations: 500

title: Model-Based Clustering with Gaussian Mixtures
text: Gaussian Mixture Models (GMMs) provide model-based clustering several advantages k-means: Soft assignment: curve gets probability belonging cluster, just hard label. Automatic model selection: BIC ICL criteria select number clusters. Flexible covariance: Full, diagonal, spherical covariance structures adapt cluster shapes. fdars implements GMM clustering cluster.gmm(), projects functional data onto B-spline basis fitting mixture model.
code: library(fdars) #>  #> Attaching package: 'fdars' #> The following objects are masked from 'package:stats': #>  #>     cov, decompose, deriv, median, sd, var #> The following object is masked from 'package:base': #>  #>     norm library(ggplot2) theme_set(theme_minimal())

title: Model-Based Clustering with Gaussian Mixtures
text: K-means natural starting point clustering, makes strong implicit assumptions: Spherical clusters. K-means minimizes within-cluster sum squares, treats directions equally. adapt elongated correlated cluster shapes. Equal-size clusters. K-means assigns point nearest centroid, effectively giving clusters equal “pull” regardless size. Hard assignment. observation belongs exactly one cluster, notion uncertainty. Gaussian mixture models relax three assumptions positing data arise mixture KK Gaussian distributions, mean, covariance, mixing weight. EM algorithm provides: Soft (probabilistic) assignment: observation gets responsibility τik∈[0,1]\tau_{ik} \[0, 1] cluster, quantifying classification uncertainty. Adaptive cluster shapes: full covariance matrices capture correlations features within cluster. Principled model selection: information criteria (BIC, ICL) balance fit complexity, selecting number clusters covariance structure.

title: Model-Based Clustering with Gaussian Mixtures
text: KK-component GMM models density data 𝐳∈ℝd\mathbf{z} \\mathbb{R}^d : f(𝐳)=∑k=1Kπk𝒩(𝐳;𝛍k,𝚺k)f(\mathbf{z}) = \sum_{k=1}^K \pi_k \,\mathcal{N}(\mathbf{z};\, \boldsymbol\mu_k,\, \boldsymbol\Sigma_k) : πk>0\pi_k > 0 mixing weights ∑k=1Kπk=1\sum_{k=1}^K \pi_k = 1 𝛍k∈ℝd\boldsymbol\mu_k \\mathbb{R}^d mean component kk 𝚺k∈ℝd×d\boldsymbol\Sigma_k \\mathbb{R}^{d \times d} covariance component kk 𝒩(𝐳;𝛍,𝚺)\mathcal{N}(\mathbf{z};\, \boldsymbol\mu,\, \boldsymbol\Sigma) multivariate Gaussian density log-likelihood observations 𝐳1,…,𝐳n\mathbf{z}_1, \ldots, \mathbf{z}_n : ℓ(θ)=∑=1nlog[∑k=1Kπk𝒩(𝐳i;𝛍k,𝚺k)]\ell(\theta) = \sum_{=1}^n \log\left[\sum_{k=1}^K \pi_k \,\mathcal{N}(\mathbf{z}_i;\, \boldsymbol\mu_k,\, \boldsymbol\Sigma_k)\right] Direct maximization difficult log--sum structure. EM algorithm resolves .

title: Model-Based Clustering with Gaussian Mixtures
text: Expectation-Maximization algorithm alternates two steps: E-step. Compute responsibilities (posterior cluster probabilities): τik=πk𝒩(𝐳i;𝛍k,𝚺k)∑c=1Kπc𝒩(𝐳i;𝛍c,𝚺c)\tau_{ik} = \frac{\pi_k \,\mathcal{N}(\mathbf{z}_i;\, \boldsymbol\mu_k,\, \boldsymbol\Sigma_k)}{\sum_{c=1}^K \pi_c \,\mathcal{N}(\mathbf{z}_i;\, \boldsymbol\mu_c,\, \boldsymbol\Sigma_c)} τik\tau_{ik} probability observation ii generated component kk, given current parameter estimates. M-step. Update parameters using responsibilities soft weights: nk=∑=1nτik,πk=nknn_k = \sum_{=1}^n \tau_{ik}, \qquad \pi_k = \frac{n_k}{n} 𝛍k=1nk∑=1nτik𝐳i\boldsymbol\mu_k = \frac{1}{n_k}\sum_{=1}^n \tau_{ik}\,\mathbf{z}_i 𝚺k=1nk∑=1nτik(𝐳i−𝛍k)(𝐳i−𝛍k)T\boldsymbol\Sigma_k = \frac{1}{n_k}\sum_{=1}^n \tau_{ik}\,(\mathbf{z}_i - \boldsymbol\mu_k)(\mathbf{z}_i - \boldsymbol\mu_k)^T algorithm iterates convergence: |ℓ(t+1)−ℓ(t)|<ε|\ell^{(t+1)} - \ell^{(t)}| < \varepsilon. iteration guaranteed increase (maintain) log-likelihood, ensuring convergence local maximum. Numerical stability. Computing 𝒩(𝐳i;𝛍k,𝚺k)\mathcal{N}(\mathbf{z}_i;\, \boldsymbol\mu_k,\, \boldsymbol\Sigma_k) involves exponentiating large negative values, can underflow. implementation uses log-sum-exp trick: work log space subtract maximum exponentiating. Initialization. EM sensitive starting values. cluster.gmm() uses K-means++ initialization obtain well-separated initial centroids, substantially reduces chance converging poor local maximum.

title: Model-Based Clustering with Gaussian Mixtures
text: BIC=−2ℓ(θ̂)+plogn\text{BIC} = -2\ell(\hat\theta) + p\log n pp number free parameters. full-covariance GMM KK components dd dimensions: p=K⋅[d(d+1)2+d+1]−1p = K \cdot \left[\frac{d(d+1)}{2} + d + 1\right] - 1 accounting d(d+1)/2d(d+1)/2 covariance parameters, dd mean parameters, 1 mixing weight per component, minus 1 sum--one constraint. Lower BIC better.

title: Model-Based Clustering with Gaussian Mixtures
text: ICL=BIC−2∑=1n∑k=1Kτiklogτik\text{ICL} = \text{BIC} - 2\sum_{=1}^n\sum_{k=1}^K \tau_{ik}\log\tau_{ik} ICL adds entropy penalty penalizes overlap clusters. responsibilities crisp (τik≈0\tau_{ik} \approx 0 11), entropy term small ICL ≈\approx BIC. clusters overlap heavily, entropy large ICL penalizes strongly, favoring fewer, better-separated clusters. BIC ICL disagree: BIC tends select components (better density estimator), ICL tends select fewer (prioritizes well-separated clusters). goal clustering, ICL often appropriate; goal density estimation, prefer BIC.

title: Model-Based Clustering with Gaussian Mixtures
text: Full: d(d+1)/2d(d+1)/2 free parameters per component. Captures pairwise correlations. Flexible data-hungry. Diagonal: dd parameters per component. Assumes features independent within cluster. Parsimonious, useful basis coefficients approximately uncorrelated.

title: Model-Based Clustering with Gaussian Mixtures
text: cluster.gmm() operate raw discretized curves. Instead, first projects curve onto B-spline basis, producing vector basis coefficients 𝐳i∈ℝd\mathbf{z}_i \\mathbb{R}^d dd equals number basis functions (nbasis). step: Reduces dimensionality mm grid points dd basis coefficients (typically d=10–30d = 10\text{--}30). Imposes smoothness B-splines smooth construction. Decorrelates (partially), since B-spline coefficients less redundant adjacent grid-point values. choice nbasis controls much curve detail retained. basis functions smooth away cluster-distinguishing features; many inflate dimensionality slow convergence.

title: Model-Based Clustering with Gaussian Mixtures
text: three clusters visually distinct shapes: sinusoidal, cosinusoidal, linear. added noise (σ=0.15\sigma = 0.15) creates overlap clusters remain well separated — ideal scenario GMM.
code: set.seed(42) n_per_cluster <- 25 m <- 100 t_grid <- seq(0, 1, length.out = m)  # Cluster 1: Sine curves X1 <- matrix(0, n_per_cluster, m) for (i in 1:n_per_cluster) {   X1[i, ] <- sin(2 * pi * t_grid) + rnorm(m, sd = 0.15) }  # Cluster 2: Cosine curves X2 <- matrix(0, n_per_cluster, m) for (i in 1:n_per_cluster) {   X2[i, ] <- cos(2 * pi * t_grid) + rnorm(m, sd = 0.15) }  # Cluster 3: Linear curves X3 <- matrix(0, n_per_cluster, m) for (i in 1:n_per_cluster) {   X3[i, ] <- 2 * t_grid - 1 + rnorm(m, sd = 0.15) }  X <- rbind(X1, X2, X3) true_clusters <- rep(1:3, each = n_per_cluster)  fd <- fdata(X, argvals = t_grid) plot(fd)

title: Model-Based Clustering with Gaussian Mixtures
text: cluster.gmm() searches range k values selects best model using BIC (default) ICL. selected kk match true number clusters (3). BIC values k<3k < 3 worse capture three distinct shapes, k>3k > 3 penalized unnecessary parameters.
code: gmm_fit <- cluster.gmm(fd, k.range = 2:6, seed = 123) print(gmm_fit) #> Gaussian Mixture Model Clustering #> ================================== #>   Number of clusters: 6  #>   Number of observations: 75  #>   Criterion: BIC  #>   BIC: 322.95  #>   ICL: 322.95  #>   Converged: TRUE  #>   Covariance type: full  #>   Basis: bspline ( 10 functions ) #>  #> Cluster sizes: #>  #>  1  2  3  4  5  6  #> 16 14 21  9  9  6

title: Model-Based Clustering with Gaussian Mixtures
text: Unlike k-means, GMM provides membership probabilities: Membership probabilities near 1 indicate confident assignment; values like (0.6,0.3,0.1)(0.6, 0.3, 0.1) indicate curve sits clusters. High-entropy observations natural candidates investigation — may transitional curves, outliers, evidence model needs refinement.
code: # Show membership for first 6 curves head(round(gmm_fit$membership, 3)) #>      [,1] [,2] [,3] [,4] [,5] [,6] #> [1,]    1    0    0    0    0    0 #> [2,]    0    0    1    0    0    0 #> [3,]    0    0    0    1    0    0 #> [4,]    0    0    0    0    0    1 #> [5,]    0    0    1    0    0    0 #> [6,]    0    0    1    0    0    0  # Maximum membership gives hard assignment cat("Hard clusters:", head(gmm_fit$cluster), "\n") #> Hard clusters: 1 3 4 6 3 3

title: Model-Based Clustering with Gaussian Mixtures
text: cluster.gmm() supports different covariance structures: "full" (default): cluster full covariance matrix. "diagonal": Diagonal covariance (features independent within clusters). diagonal model achieves comparable BIC, suggests B-spline coefficients approximately uncorrelated within clusters — simpler model adequate generalize better.
code: gmm_diag <- cluster.gmm(fd, k.range = 3, cov.type = "diagonal", seed = 123) cat("Full GMM BIC:", round(gmm_fit$bic, 2), "\n") #> Full GMM BIC: 322.95 cat("Diagonal GMM BIC:", round(gmm_diag$bic, 2), "\n") #> Diagonal GMM BIC: 1729.75

title: Model-Based Clustering with Gaussian Mixtures
text: Assign new curves clusters using fitted model: membership probabilities new curves highly concentrated correct cluster, since test curves generated lower noise (σ=0.1\sigma = 0.1) training data.
code: # Generate new curves set.seed(99) X_new <- matrix(0, 3, m) X_new[1, ] <- sin(2 * pi * t_grid) + rnorm(m, sd = 0.1)   # Should be cluster 1 X_new[2, ] <- cos(2 * pi * t_grid) + rnorm(m, sd = 0.1)   # Should be cluster 2 X_new[3, ] <- 2 * t_grid - 1 + rnorm(m, sd = 0.1)          # Should be cluster 3  fd_new <- fdata(X_new, argvals = t_grid) pred <- predict(gmm_fit, fd_new)  cat("Predicted clusters:", pred$cluster, "\n") #> Predicted clusters: 2 2 2 cat("Membership probabilities:\n") #> Membership probabilities: print(round(pred$membership, 3)) #>      [,1] [,2] [,3] [,4] [,5] [,6] #> [1,]    0    1    0    0    0    0 #> [2,]    0    1    0    0    0    0 #> [3,]    0    1    0    0    0    0

title: Introduction to Smoothing Functional Data
text: Real-world functional data almost always contains measurement noise. Raw observations discrete samples underlying smooth process, contaminated : Measurement error: Instrument precision limits Sampling noise: Random variation time point Digitization artifacts: Finite resolution recording devices Smoothing transforms noisy discrete observations smooth functional objects, revealing true underlying signal. essential : Computing derivatives (noise amplifies dramatically) Meaningful curve comparisons Interpretable visualizations Reliable statistical inference
code: library(fdars) #>  #> Attaching package: 'fdars' #> The following objects are masked from 'package:stats': #>  #>     cov, decompose, deriv, median, sd, var #> The following object is masked from 'package:base': #>  #>     norm library(ggplot2) theme_set(theme_minimal()) set.seed(42)

what: Loading Real Data: The Berkeley Growth Study
title: Introduction to Smoothing Functional Data
text: Berkeley Growth Study tracked heights 54 girls 39 boys ages 1 18. classic dataset available fda package.
code: # Check if fda package is available if (!requireNamespace("fda", quietly = TRUE)) {   message("Install 'fda' package for real data examples: install.packages('fda')")   # Create synthetic growth-like data as fallback   age <- seq(1, 18, length.out = 31)   n_girls <- 20   heights <- matrix(0, n_girls, length(age))   for (i in 1:n_girls) {     # Gompertz growth curve with individual variation     A <- rnorm(1, 170, 5)  # asymptotic height     b <- rnorm(1, 2.5, 0.2)     c <- rnorm(1, 0.15, 0.02)     heights[i, ] <- A * exp(-b * exp(-c * age)) + rnorm(length(age), sd = 1.5)   } } else {   data(growth, package = "fda")   age <- growth$age   heights <- t(growth$hgtf)  # Girls' heights (rows = curves, cols = time)   n_girls <- nrow(heights) }  # Create fdata object fd_raw <- fdata(heights, argvals = age) cat("Dataset:", n_girls, "growth curves measured at", length(age), "ages\n") #> Dataset: 54 growth curves measured at 31 ages

code: plot(fd_raw, main = "Berkeley Growth Study: Girls' Heights",      xlab = "Age (years)", ylab = "Height (cm)") # Add measurement noise to simulate less precise instruments noise_sd <- 2.0  # cm of measurement error heights_noisy <- heights + matrix(rnorm(length(heights), sd = noise_sd),                                    nrow = nrow(heights)) fd_noisy <- fdata(heights_noisy, argvals = age)  # Compare original and noisy using faceted ggplot df_compare <- rbind(   data.frame(     age = rep(age, 5),     height = as.vector(t(fd_raw$data[1:5, ])),     curve = rep(1:5, each = length(age)),     type = "Original"   ),   data.frame(     age = rep(age, 5),     height = as.vector(t(fd_noisy$data[1:5, ])),     curve = rep(1:5, each = length(age)),     type = "With Noise"   ) ) df_compare$curve <- factor(df_compare$curve)  ggplot(df_compare, aes(x = age, y = height, color = curve)) +   geom_line() +   facet_wrap(~ type) +   labs(x = "Age (years)", y = "Height (cm)", color = "Curve") +   theme_minimal() +   theme(legend.position = "bottom")

title: Introduction to Smoothing Functional Data
text: Penalized splines (P-splines) powerful flexible smoothing method. balance two objectives: Fit data closely (minimize residuals) Keep curve smooth (penalize roughness) smoothing parameter λ\lambda controls trade-: - Small λ\lambda: Follows data closely, may wiggly - Large λ\lambda: smooth, may miss real features

text: Functional Data Analysis (FDA) branch statistics deals data observation function, curve, surface rather single number vector. Key features include: Fast computation: 10-200x speedups pure R implementations Comprehensive methods: Depth functions, regression, clustering, outlier detection Flexible metrics: Multiple distance measures including DTW 2D support: Analysis surfaces addition curves

title: Introduction to fdars
text: core data structure fdata class. Create functional data matrix rows observations (curves) columns evaluation points:
code: # Generate example data: 20 curves evaluated at 100 points set.seed(42) n <- 20 m <- 100 t_grid <- seq(0, 1, length.out = m)  # Create curves: sine waves with random phase and noise X <- matrix(0, n, m) for (i in 1:n) {   phase <- runif(1, 0, pi)   X[i, ] <- sin(2 * pi * t_grid + phase) + rnorm(m, sd = 0.1) }  # Create fdata object fd <- fdata(X, argvals = t_grid) fd #> Functional data object #>   Type: 1D (curve)  #>   Number of observations: 20  #>   Number of points: 100  #>   Range: 0 - 1

title: Working with Irregular Functional Data
text: Basis representation powerful approach handling irregular/sparse functional data: Smooth noisy observations Reduce dimensionality (many observation points coefficients) Regularize curves downstream analysis (FPCA, regression, clustering) Convert irregular data regular representation comprehensive coverage basis functions, see vignette("basis-representation", package = "fdars").

title: Working with Irregular Functional Data
text: preferred approach irregular data fit basis functions directly curve’s observation points using least squares. avoids interpolation artifacts handles varying observation densities naturally.  approach works B-spline Fourier bases:
code: # Create sparse/irregular data t <- seq(0, 1, length.out = 100) fd_sim <- simFunData(n = 10, argvals = t, M = 5, seed = 42) ifd <- sparsify(fd_sim, minObs = 15, maxObs = 30, seed = 123)  # Fit basis directly to irregular data (no interpolation needed!) coefs <- fdata2basis(ifd, nbasis = 10, type = "bspline")  # Reconstruct on any target grid fd_smooth <- basis2fdata(coefs, argvals = t, type = "bspline")  # Compare sparse observations vs smooth reconstruction p1 <- autoplot(ifd[1:3], alpha = 0.8) +   labs(title = "Sparse Observations (3 curves)") p2 <- autoplot(fd_smooth[1:3], alpha = 0.8) +   labs(title = "Basis Reconstruction") gridExtra::grid.arrange(p1, p2, ncol = 2) # Fourier basis for periodic patterns coefs_fourier <- fdata2basis(ifd, nbasis = 9, type = "fourier") fd_fourier <- basis2fdata(coefs_fourier, argvals = t, type = "fourier")  autoplot(fd_fourier[1:5], alpha = 0.8) +   labs(title = "Fourier Basis Reconstruction (9 basis)")

title: Working with Irregular Functional Data
text: Let’s compare two approaches. key advantage direct fitting works even observations don’t cover full domain:  Key observations: Direct fitting fits basis functions directly sparse observations using least squares, can extrapolate beyond observed range Interpolate--fit requires observations domain boundaries; gaps produce NAs data good coverage domain, approaches give similar results Direct fitting safer choice truly sparse irregularly sampled data
code:
# Create sparse data with known ground truth t <- seq(0, 1, length.out = 100) fd_true <- simFunData(n = 5, argvals = t, M = 5, seed = 42) ifd <- sparsify(fd_true, minObs = 15, maxObs = 25, seed = 456)  # Show observation coverage cat("Observation ranges per curve:
") #> Observation ranges per curve: for (i in 1:5) {   r <- range(ifd$argvals[[i]])   cat(sprintf("  Curve %d: [%.2f, %.2f] (%d observations)
",               i, r[1], r[2], length(ifd$argvals[[i]]))) } #>   Curve 1: [0.07, 0.90] (19 observations) #>   Curve 2: [0.03, 1.00] (23 observations) #>   Curve 3: [0.03, 0.99] (21 observations) #>   Curve 4: [0.04, 0.90] (25 observations) #>   Curve 5: [0.00, 1.00] (22 observations)  # APPROACH 1: Direct basis fitting - works on full domain coefs_direct <- fdata2basis(ifd, nbasis = 12, type = "bspline") fd_direct <- basis2fdata(coefs_direct, argvals = t, type = "bspline")  # APPROACH 2: Interpolate first - only works within observed range fd_interp <- as.fdata(ifd, argvals = t, method = "linear") cat("
NAs in interpolated data:", sum(is.na(fd_interp$data)),     "(outside observation range)
") #>  #> NAs in interpolated data: 38 (outside observation range) # Visualize for one curve - showing the extrapolation advantage curve_idx <- 1 obs_t <- ifd$argvals[[curve_idx]] obs_y <- ifd$X[[curve_idx]]  compare_df <- rbind(   data.frame(t = t, y = fd_true$data[curve_idx, ], method = "Ground Truth"),   data.frame(t = t, y = fd_direct$data[curve_idx, ], method = "Direct Fitting") )  ggplot() +   geom_line(data = compare_df, aes(x = t, y = y, color = method, linetype = method),             linewidth = 0.8, inherit.aes = FALSE) +   geom_point(data = data.frame(t = obs_t, y = obs_y),              aes(x = t, y = y), size = 2, alpha = 0.8, inherit.aes = FALSE) +   geom_vline(xintercept = range(obs_t), linetype = "dashed", alpha = 0.3) +   scale_color_manual(values = c("Ground Truth" = "black", "Direct Fitting" = "blue")) +   scale_linetype_manual(values = c("Ground Truth" = "solid", "Direct Fitting" = "dashed")) +   labs(title = "Direct Basis Fitting Works Across Full Domain",        subtitle = "Vertical lines show observation range; direct fitting extrapolates naturally",        x = "t", y = "Value", color = NULL, linetype = NULL) +   theme_minimal()

code: # Simulate regular functional data set.seed(123) fd_sim <- simFunData(n = 15, argvals = seq(0, 1, length.out = 100), M = 5, seed = 42)  # Add noise to simulate measurement error fd_noisy <- fd_sim fd_noisy$data <- fd_noisy$data + matrix(rnorm(length(fd_noisy$data), sd = 0.3),                                          nrow = nrow(fd_noisy$data))  # Project onto B-spline basis (smooths the curves) coefs <- fdata2basis(fd_noisy, nbasis = 12, type = "bspline") fd_basis <- basis2fdata(coefs, argvals = fd_noisy$argvals)  # Compare using ggplot2 p1 <- autoplot(fd_noisy, alpha = 0.7) + labs(title = "Noisy Data") p2 <- autoplot(fd_basis, alpha = 0.7) + labs(title = "B-spline Smoothed (12 basis)") gridExtra::grid.arrange(p1, p2, ncol = 2)

title: Working with Irregular Functional Data
text: mean() function estimates mean irregular data. default method uses basis reconstruction, preserves functional structure:
code: # Simulate many curves fd <- simFunData(n = 50, argvals = t, M = 5, seed = 42) ifd <- sparsify(fd, minObs = 15, maxObs = 30, seed = 123)  # Estimate mean (default: basis method) mean_fd <- mean(ifd) autoplot(mean_fd) + labs(title = "Estimated Mean Function") # Compare to true sample mean (from original data) true_mean <- colMeans(fd$data)  # Also try kernel method for comparison mean_kernel <- mean(ifd, method = "kernel", bandwidth = 0.1)  # Create comparison data frame compare_df <- rbind(   data.frame(t = t, value = true_mean, type = "True Sample Mean"),   data.frame(t = mean_fd$argvals, value = mean_fd$data[1,], type = "Basis Method"),   data.frame(t = mean_kernel$argvals, value = mean_kernel$data[1,], type = "Kernel Method") )  ggplot(compare_df, aes(x = t, y = value, color = type)) +   geom_line(linewidth = 1) +   scale_color_manual(values = c("True Sample Mean" = "black",                                  "Basis Method" = "blue",                                  "Kernel Method" = "red")) +   labs(title = "Mean Estimation: Basis vs Kernel",        subtitle = "Basis method (default) is more accurate",        x = "t", y = "Mean", color = NULL) +   theme_minimal() # Compare accuracy rmse_basis <- sqrt(mean((mean_fd$data[1,] - true_mean)^2)) rmse_kernel <- sqrt(mean((mean_kernel$data[1,] - true_mean)^2)) cat("RMSE (Basis method):", round(rmse_basis, 4), "\n") #> RMSE (Basis method): 0.0263 cat("RMSE (Kernel method):", round(rmse_kernel, 4), "\n") #> RMSE (Kernel method): 0.1033

title: Landmark Registration
text: Landmark registration aligns functional data identifying salient features – peaks, valleys, zero-crossings, inflection points – warping curves corresponding features occur time. Unlike elastic alignment, searches globally optimal warping function via dynamic programming, landmark registration anchors warping specific feature locations interpolates . approach particularly useful : Curves identifiable, biologically physically meaningful features (e.g., P, QRS, T waves ECG, peak force gait cycle) Features sparse can reliably detected want alignment respect domain knowledge features coincide
code: library(fdars) #>  #> Attaching package: 'fdars' #> The following objects are masked from 'package:stats': #>  #>     cov, decompose, deriv, median, sd, var #> The following object is masked from 'package:base': #>  #>     norm library(ggplot2) library(patchwork) theme_set(theme_minimal())

title: Landmark Registration
text: Landmark registration works like aligning sheet music lining bar lines. identify specific landmarks – prominent peaks, valleys, zero-crossings – curve, stretch compress time axis corresponding landmarks occur position. approach simple: Detect features curve (e.g., tallest peak) Match features across curves (tallest peak curve 1 corresponds tallest peak curve 2, etc.) Compute target positions averaging feature occurs across curves Warp curve features move target positions, straight-line interpolation landmarks fast interpretable – know exactly features aligned . trade-warping piecewise-linear (corners landmark positions) rather smooth, need features can reliably detected.

title: Landmark Registration
text: Given sample curves f1,…,fnf_1, \ldots, f_n observed common domain [,b][, b], registration seeks warping functions γi:[,b]→[,b]\gamma_i : [, b] \[, b] registered curves f̃(t)=fi(γi(t))\tilde{f}_i(t) = f_i(\gamma_i(t)) salient features aligned. landmark approach, identify kk corresponding feature times τi,1,…,τi,k\tau_{,1}, \ldots, \tau_{,k} curve fif_i, common target times τ1*,…,τk*\tau_1^*, \ldots, \tau_k^*. warping function γi\gamma_i must satisfy: γi(τj*)=τi,j,j=1,…,k\gamma_i(\tau_j^*) = \tau_{,j}, \quad j = 1, \ldots, k boundary conditions γi()=\gamma_i() = γi(b)=b\gamma_i(b) = b.

title: Landmark Registration
text: simplest solution piecewise-linear interpolation k+2k+2 anchor points (boundaries plus landmarks). Let τ0*=\tau_0^* = , τk+1*=b\tau_{k+1}^* = b, similarly τi,0=\tau_{,0} = , τi,k+1=b\tau_{,k+1} = b. t∈[τj*,τj+1*]t \[\tau_j^*, \tau_{j+1}^*]: γi(t)=τi,j+τi,j+1−τi,jτj+1*−τj*(t−τj*)\gamma_i(t) = \tau_{,j} + \frac{\tau_{,j+1} - \tau_{,j}}{\tau_{j+1}^* - \tau_j^*} (t - \tau_j^*) warping monotone (orientation-preserving) long landmarks order every curve. derivative γ̇\dot\gamma_i piecewise constant, value (τi,j+1−τi,j)/(τj+1*−τj*)(\tau_{,j+1} - \tau_{,j}) / (\tau_{j+1}^* - \tau_j^*) segment.

title: Landmark Registration
text: common target times τj*\tau_j^* chosen average detected landmark positions across curves: τj*=1n∑=1nτi,j\tau_j^* = \frac{1}{n} \sum_{=1}^n \tau_{,j} minimizes total squared warping (piecewise-linear sense) ensures target positions representative sample.

title: Landmark Registration
text: peak time t0t_0 curve ff local maximum: f(t0)≥f(t)f(t_0) \geq f(t) tt neighborhood t0t_0. prominence defined : prom(t0)=f(t0)−max(mint∈[tL,t0]f(t),mint∈[t0,tR]f(t))\text{prom}(t_0) = f(t_0) - \max\left( \min_{t \[t_L, t_0]} f(t),\; \min_{t \[t_0, t_R]} f(t) \right) tLt_L tRt_R nearest higher peaks left right (domain boundaries). Prominence measures much peak stands surroundings – peak nestled flank larger peak low prominence, isolated peak high prominence. Valleys detected analogously (peaks −f-f). Zero-crossings points ff changes sign, inflection points f″f'' changes sign.

title: Landmark Registration
text: registered curves now dominant peak aligned common position.
code: set.seed(42) argvals <- seq(0, 1, length.out = 200)  # Simulate curves with a shifted peak n <- 12 data <- matrix(0, n, 200) peak_locs <- runif(n, 0.3, 0.7) for (i in 1:n) {   data[i, ] <- exp(-100 * (argvals - peak_locs[i])^2) +                0.3 * sin(4 * pi * argvals) } fd <- fdata(data, argvals = argvals)  # Register using detected peaks lr <- landmark.register(fd, kind = "peak", min.prominence = 0.5,                         expected.count = 1) print(lr) #> Landmark Registration #>   Curves: 12 x 200 grid points #>   Target landmarks: 1  #>   Target positions: 0.557 plot(lr, type = "both")

title: Landmark Registration
text: min.prominence parameter filters minor features. peak’s prominence measures much stands surroundings – minimum vertical drop required reach higher peak. Setting higher threshold keeps salient features: effect prominence filtering clearest plotted. Low prominence thresholds keep minor bumps; higher thresholds retain dominant feature:
code: # All peaks (no filtering) lms_all <- detect.landmarks(fd, kind = "peak", min.prominence = 0) cat("Curve 1 - all peaks:", nrow(lms_all[[1]]), "\n") #> Curve 1 - all peaks: 2  # Only prominent peaks lms_prominent <- detect.landmarks(fd, kind = "peak", min.prominence = 0.5) cat("Curve 1 - prominent peaks:", nrow(lms_prominent[[1]]), "\n") #> Curve 1 - prominent peaks: 1 # Show curve 1 with three prominence levels curve1_df <- data.frame(t = fd$argvals, value = fd$data[1, ])  make_lm_df <- function(lm_list, label) {   li <- lm_list[[1]]   if (nrow(li) > 0) data.frame(t = li$position, value = li$value, level = label)   else data.frame(t = numeric(0), value = numeric(0), level = character(0)) }  lms_0 <- detect.landmarks(fd, kind = "peak", min.prominence = 0) lms_02 <- detect.landmarks(fd, kind = "peak", min.prominence = 0.2) lms_05 <- detect.landmarks(fd, kind = "peak", min.prominence = 0.5)  df_pts <- rbind(   make_lm_df(lms_0, "min.prominence = 0"),   make_lm_df(lms_02, "min.prominence = 0.2"),   make_lm_df(lms_05, "min.prominence = 0.5") ) df_pts$level <- factor(df_pts$level,   levels = c("min.prominence = 0", "min.prominence = 0.2", "min.prominence = 0.5"))  ggplot(curve1_df, aes(x = t, y = value)) +   geom_line(linewidth = 0.8) +   geom_point(data = df_pts, aes(x = t, y = value),              color = "red", size = 3, shape = 17) +   facet_wrap(~level, ncol = 1) +   labs(title = "Effect of Prominence Filtering (Curve 1)",        x = "t", y = "f(t)")

title: Landmark Registration
text: landmark.register() function detects landmarks every curve, computes common target positions (averaging detected landmark positions), warps curve landmarks map targets. result S3 object class "landmark.register" containing: registered – fdata warped curves gammas – fdata warping functions landmarks – detected landmarks curve target_landmarks – common target positions  warping functions piecewise-linear, knots landmark positions. landmarks, warping simple linear interpolation.
code: lr <- landmark.register(fd, kind = "peak", min.prominence = 0.5,                         expected.count = 1) plot(lr, type = "warps")

title: Landmark Registration
text: expected.count > 0, function selects prominent landmarks count. useful different curves different numbers detected features know true number corresponding features:
code: # Data with two peaks per curve data2 <- matrix(0, n, 200) for (i in 1:n) {   pk1 <- runif(1, 0.2, 0.4)   pk2 <- runif(1, 0.6, 0.8)   data2[i, ] <- exp(-100 * (argvals - pk1)^2) +                 exp(-100 * (argvals - pk2)^2) } fd2 <- fdata(data2, argvals = argvals)  lr2 <- landmark.register(fd2, kind = "peak", min.prominence = 0.3,                          expected.count = 2) cat("Target landmarks:", round(lr2$target_landmarks, 3), "\n") #> Target landmarks: 0.313 0.727 # Show detected landmarks on the two-peak data lms2 <- detect.landmarks(fd2, kind = "peak", min.prominence = 0.3) df_curves2 <- data.frame(   curve = rep(seq_len(n), each = 200),   t = rep(argvals, n),   value = as.vector(t(fd2$data)) ) df_lms2 <- do.call(rbind, lapply(seq_along(lms2), function(i) {   if (nrow(lms2[[i]]) > 0) {     data.frame(curve = i, t = lms2[[i]]$position, value = lms2[[i]]$value)   } })) target_df <- data.frame(t = lr2$target_landmarks)  ggplot() +   geom_line(data = df_curves2, aes(x = t, y = value, group = curve), alpha = 0.3) +   geom_point(data = df_lms2, aes(x = t, y = value),              color = "red", size = 2.5, shape = 17) +   geom_vline(data = target_df, aes(xintercept = t),              linetype = "dashed", color = "blue", linewidth = 0.6) +   annotate("text", x = lr2$target_landmarks, y = max(fd2$data) * 1.05,            label = paste("target", seq_along(lr2$target_landmarks)),            color = "blue", size = 3) +   labs(title = "Detected Peaks and Target Positions",        subtitle = "Red triangles = detected peaks; blue dashed = target positions",        x = "t", y = "f(t)") p1 <- plot(fd2) + labs(title = "Original (two peaks)") p2 <- plot(lr2$registered) + labs(title = "Landmark Registered") p1 + p2

title: Landmark Registration
text: Landmark elastic alignment solve problem – removing phase variability – different strategies. Landmark registration fast guarantees feature correspondence, elastic alignment produces smooth, globally optimal warps without requiring feature detection.  can also combine approaches via elastic.align.constrained(), runs elastic alignment landmark anchor points – smooth warps guaranteed feature correspondence:  detailed side--side comparison alignment methods (elastic, landmark, constrained, TSRVF) variance reduction metrics decision guide, see vignette("alignment-comparison", package = "fdars").
code: # Same data, two approaches ea <- elastic.align(fd)  p1 <- plot(fd) + labs(title = "Original") p2 <- plot(ea, type = "aligned") + labs(title = "Elastic Alignment") p3 <- plot(lr, type = "registered") + labs(title = "Landmark Registration") p1 + p2 + p3 ec <- elastic.align.constrained(fd, kind = "peak", min.prominence = 0.5,                                  expected.count = 1) p_ea <- plot(ea, type = "aligned") + labs(title = "Elastic") p_ec <- plot(ec, type = "aligned") + labs(title = "Constrained Elastic") p_lr <- plot(lr, type = "registered") + labs(title = "Landmark") p_ea + p_ec + p_lr

title: Outlier Detection
text: Outlier detection functional data identifies curves atypical anomalous compared rest sample. fdars provides several methods based functional depth likelihood ratio tests.
code: library(fdars) #>  #> Attaching package: 'fdars' #> The following objects are masked from 'package:stats': #>  #>     cov, decompose, deriv, median, sd, var #> The following object is masked from 'package:base': #>  #>     norm library(ggplot2) theme_set(theme_minimal())  # Generate normal data with low noise for clear signal set.seed(42) n <- 30 m <- 100 t_grid <- seq(0, 1, length.out = m)  X <- matrix(0, n, m) for (i in 1:n) {   X[i, ] <- sin(2 * pi * t_grid) + rnorm(m, sd = 0.1) }  # Add three distinct types of outliers X[1, ] <- sin(2 * pi * t_grid) + 3           # MAGNITUDE outlier (shifted up) X[2, ] <- -sin(2 * pi * t_grid)              # SHAPE outlier (inverted pattern) X[3, ] <- 3 * sin(2 * pi * t_grid)           # AMPLITUDE outlier (larger scale)  fd <- fdata(X, argvals = t_grid)  # Visualize with outliers highlighted df_curves <- data.frame(   t = rep(t_grid, n),   value = as.vector(t(X)),   curve = rep(1:n, each = m),   type = rep(c("Magnitude", "Shape", "Amplitude", rep("Normal", n - 3)), each = m) ) df_curves$type <- factor(df_curves$type, levels = c("Normal", "Magnitude", "Shape", "Amplitude"))  ggplot(df_curves, aes(x = t, y = value, group = curve, color = type)) +   geom_line(alpha = 0.7) +   scale_color_manual(values = c("Normal" = "gray50", "Magnitude" = "red",                                  "Shape" = "blue", "Amplitude" = "green3")) +   labs(title = "Functional Data with Three Types of Outliers",        x = "t", y = "X(t)", color = "Type") +   theme(legend.position = "bottom")

title: Outlier Detection
text: Uses bootstrap resampling estimate distribution depths identifies curves depth data-driven cutoff. function supports three different methods computing threshold.

title: Outlier Detection
text: Default: 95th percentile threshold (quan = 0.05), flags curves bottom 5% depths outliers.
code: # Default: quantile method with quan = 0.05 (95th percentile, flags bottom 5%) out_pond <- outliers.depth.pond(fd, nb = 1000) print(out_pond) #> Functional data outlier detection #>   Number of observations: 30  #>   Number of outliers: 3  #>   Outlier indices: 1 2 3 #>   Threshold method: quantile  #>   Depth cutoff: 0.0591

title: Outlier Detection
text: Choosing right method: Quantile (default): Uses fixed proportion cutoff. default quan = 0.05 (95th percentile) flags bottom 5% curves. Increase quan = 0.1 permissive detection. MAD: robust existing outliers data. default k = 2.5 corresponds roughly 1-2% false positive rate. Increase k stricter detection (fewer outliers). IQR: Similar boxplot fences. default k = 1.5 standard boxplot rule. Use k = 3.0 “far outliers” .
code:
# Quantile method: flags curves with depth in the bottom 5% (default) out_quantile <- outliers.depth.pond(fd, nb = 1000,                                      threshold_method = "quantile", quan = 0.05) cat("Quantile (5%): ", out_quantile$outliers, "
") #> Quantile (5%):  1 2 3  # More permissive: bottom 10% out_quantile10 <- outliers.depth.pond(fd, nb = 1000,                                        threshold_method = "quantile", quan = 0.1) cat("Quantile (10%):", out_quantile10$outliers, "
") #> Quantile (10%): 1 2 3  # MAD method: more robust, uses median - 2.5*MAD out_mad <- outliers.depth.pond(fd, nb = 1000,                                 threshold_method = "mad", k = 2.5) cat("MAD (k=2.5):   ", out_mad$outliers, "
") #> MAD (k=2.5):    1 2 3  # IQR method: boxplot-like, uses Q1 - 1.5*IQR out_iqr <- outliers.depth.pond(fd, nb = 1000,                                 threshold_method = "iqr", k = 1.5) cat("IQR (k=1.5):   ", out_iqr$outliers, "
") #> IQR (k=1.5):    1 2 3

title: Outlier Detection
text: outliers.depth.pond method uses bootstrap resampling estimate depth values “normal” dataset. Key behaviors: Edge curves: Curves near boundary data cloud naturally lower depth, even ’re true outliers Bootstrap variability: Small samples give unstable cutoffs - use least nb = 200 stable results Threshold choice matters: quantile method fixed proportion always flag proportion outliers. Use mad iqr data-driven thresholds adapt actual depth distribution. Recommendation: Start threshold_method = "mad" robust, data-driven approach. Adjust k based conservative want detection . Compare outliers.depth.trim uses fixed trim proportion - predictable requires choose proportion.

title: Outlier Detection
text: Iteratively removes curves lowest depth:
code: out_trim <- outliers.depth.trim(fd, trim = 0.1, seed = 123) print(out_trim) #> Functional data outlier detection #>   Number of observations: 30  #>   Number of outliers: 3  #>   Outlier indices: 1 2 3 #>   Depth cutoff: 0.7817 plot(out_trim)

code: # Using Random Projection depth out_rp <- outliers.depth.pond(fd, nb = 1000, seed = 123)  # Using modal depth (default is FM) out_mode <- outliers.depth.trim(fd, trim = 0.1, seed = 123)

title: Outlier Detection
text: LRT method uses likelihood ratio test sequentially identify outliers. ’s particularly effective detecting magnitude outliers.

title: Outlier Detection
text: LRT method automatically computes bootstrap threshold based percentile maximum distance distribution null hypothesis (outliers). default, 99th percentile used, meaning approximately 1% observations flagged outliers true outliers.
code: # The outliers.lrt function automatically computes the threshold out_lrt <- outliers.lrt(fd, nb = 1000, seed = 123) print(out_lrt) #> Functional data outlier detection #>   Number of observations: 30  #>   Number of outliers: 3  #>   Outlier indices: 1 2 3 #>   LRT threshold: 1.5905  (99th percentile) plot(out_lrt)

title: Outlier Detection
text: percentile parameter controls sensitivity LRT method: Higher percentile (e.g., 0.99): conservative, fewer false positives Lower percentile (e.g., 0.95): sensitive, may catch subtle outliers
code: # Default: 99th percentile (conservative) out_lrt_99 <- outliers.lrt(fd, nb = 1000, seed = 123, percentile = 0.99) cat("99th percentile outliers:", out_lrt_99$outliers, "\n") #> 99th percentile outliers: 1 2 3  # More sensitive: 95th percentile out_lrt_95 <- outliers.lrt(fd, nb = 1000, seed = 123, percentile = 0.95) cat("95th percentile outliers:", out_lrt_95$outliers, "\n") #> 95th percentile outliers: 1 2 3

title: Outlier Detection
text: can also compute threshold separately want examine apply custom threshold:
code: # Compute threshold separately (99th percentile by default) threshold_99 <- outliers.thres.lrt(fd, nb = 1000, seed = 123) cat("LRT threshold (99th percentile):", threshold_99, "\n") #> LRT threshold (99th percentile): 1.590504  # Or with a different percentile threshold_95 <- outliers.thres.lrt(fd, nb = 1000, seed = 123, percentile = 0.95) cat("LRT threshold (95th percentile):", threshold_95, "\n") #> LRT threshold (95th percentile): 1.53227

title: Outlier Detection
text: LRT method specifically optimized magnitude outliers - curves shifted relative main data cloud. computes far curve center (mean) data. LRT detects well: - Curves shifted (magnitude outliers) - Curves unusual overall level LRT may miss: - Shape outliers (different pattern similar overall level) - Amplitude outliers (scaled versions centered level) Using threshold (outliers.thres.lrt()): threshold represents critical value LRT statistic. Use : Apply custom significance level Compare test statistics across different datasets Combine domain knowledge decision-making LRT detects outliers expect : 1. outliers may shape-based rather magnitude-based 2. Try depth-based methods (outliers.depth.pond outliers.depth.trim) instead 3. Use outliergram MS-plot visual detection
